title: Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries
authors: Fokkema T, van Damme AADN, Fornerod MWJ, de Vos RJ, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, van Middelkoop M
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: Recreational half-marathon (n=556) and marathon (n=441) participants who completed three questionnaires
findings: Half marathon: weekly training >32 km (beta -4.19, 95% CI -6.52 to -1.85) and longest run >21 km (beta -3.87, 95% CI -6.31 to -1.44) were associated with a faster finish time, and with less pace decline (beta -1.81 and -1.89).
Marathon: <40 km/wk was related to a slower finish (beta 6.33, 95% CI 0.18 to 12.48); >65 km/wk to a faster finish (beta -14.09, 95% CI -22.47 to -5.72).
Marathon: longest run <25 km was associated with a slower finish (beta 13.44, 95% CI 5.34 to 21.55).
No associations between training characteristics and running-related injuries were identified.
limitations: Self-reported volume and longest run, categorised exposures, confounding by experience and ability, finish-time units not stated in the abstract, lower CI bound for the <40 km finding is near zero, and the null injury result may reflect low power or survivor bias.
implications: Use volume and long-run values as quality floors, not caps: half >32 km/wk and longest run >21 km; marathon avoid <40 km/wk and longest run <25 km.
Weekly volume above 65 km was linked to the fastest marathon group; still progress gradually.
